abstract: Despite the utility of Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) in discrete optimization, developing iterative workflows remains cumbersome due to fragmented, low-level solver APIs. We present Hermax, a unified Python library and modelling compiler for MaxSAT. Hermax provides an IPAMIR interface that exposes incremental solving, assumptions, and weight updates through a single API across many incremental and non-incremental backends. Furthermore, it introduces a compiler with Constraint Programming primitives that translates high-level models directly into optimized CNF/WCNF through eager evaluation. This compiler allows automatic optimizations like integer ladder graph encoding that bypasses Pseudo-Boolean formulation when possible. Together, these features enable rapid prototyping and production grade optimization directly from Python across major platforms and hardware architectures.

      Abstract
Despite the utility of Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) in discrete optimization, developing iterative
workflows remains cumbersome due to fragmented, low-level solver APIs. We present Hermax, a
unified Python library and modelling compiler for MaxSAT. Hermax provides an IPAMIR interface
that exposes incremental solving, assumptions, and weight updates through a single API across many
incremental and non-incremental backends. Furthermore, it introduces a compiler with Constraint
Programming primitives that translates high-level models directly into optimized CNF/WCNF
through eager evaluation. This compiler allows automatic optimizations like integer ladder graph
encoding that bypasses Pseudo-Boolean formulation when possible. Together, these features enable
rapid prototyping and production grade optimization directly from Python across major platforms
and hardware architectures.

 1      Introduction

In the last twenty years, the efficiency of SAT solvers has enjoyed great success [4, 26], driven
by optimized incremental Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) engines such as Glucose,
COMiniSatPS, and CaDiCaL [10, 53, 17]. Maximum Satisfiability [18] builds upon this
success to find assignments that satisfy all hard constraints while maximizing the weight of
satisfied soft constraints. However, the development of applications utilizing these engines
remains hindered by the low-level programmatic interface that must be used.

           Simultaneously, Python has emerged as one of the most preferred programming languages
       for rapid development of applications because of its straightforward syntax. While the SAT
       community has seen successful integration of Python libraries, MaxSAT prototyping has
       remained dispersed [64].

       1.1    Contributions
       In this paper, we present Hermax, a unified library that brings together decades of advances
       in MaxSAT solving in an accessible Python package. Our contributions with Hermax in this
       paper are:
           Python IPAMIR API. Hermax abstracts the differences over numerous incremental
           and non-incremental MaxSAT engines. This is possible by adopting an IPAMIR interface
           as designed in [52]. Adopting this interface allows users to swap backends without
           altering application logic and do so efficiently through a Python API. Bindings or
           reimplementations of Cardinality, Pseudo-Boolean (PB) and PB(AMO) constraints are
           also incorporated for low level manipulation.
           CP to MaxSAT Compiler. We provide a modelling compiler that translates Constraint
           Programming (CP) primitives directly into optimized CNF/WCNF. We document efficient
           integer equation encoding by graph implication of the ladder encoding, which allows us
           to bypass PB encoders for many affine constraints. The compiler supports incremental
           queries, floating and negative objectives, and lexicographic strategies.
           Distribution, Examples, and Documentation. We distribute precompiled wheels
           via PyPI for Windows, Linux, and macOS across both x86 and ARM architectures. This
           required solver specific patching and extensive testing. Moreover, we provide online
           documentation on the internals and over 30 optimization examples.


        2    Related Works
       High-level Python interfaces are ubiquitous across optimization, supported natively by solvers
       for MILP (CPLEX, Gurobi, HiGHS [31], PuLP [60, 36], SCIP [2, 44]), CP (CP-SAT [57],
       PyChoco [43]), and SMT (Z3 [23], cvc5 [13]), alongside modelling layers like MiniZinc [50],
       Pyomo [28], CVXPY [24], and CPMpy [27].
           Among these systems, CPMpy is the closest point of comparison to Hermax because
       it offers a Python CP modelling layer with a MaxSAT target. However, CPMpy exhibits
       limitations: its MaxSAT capability is restricted to non-incremental RC2 and it relies on a
       generic decomposition pipeline where integer arithmetic is linearized via one-hot encodings.
           In the Boolean domain, several libraries exist. PySAT [32] provides a toolkit for SAT
       prototyping with bindings for solvers and cardinality encodings. OptiLog [8] provides a Python
       framework for developing SAT-based systems, allowing dynamic loading of incremental SAT
       solvers and modelling of non-CNF formats [3] and PB support. RustSAT [37] is a modern
       library with Rust and Python Bindings, which, similar to PySAT, provides access to state of
       the art SAT solvers and includes various cardinality and PB encodings and utilities. However,
       all three libraries operate at the propositional solver level.
           Despite two decades of Maximum Satisfiability research and the annual MaxSAT Evalu-
       ation [9, 16], the Python ecosystem lacks a high performance library dedicated to MaxSAT.
       Most prominently, the well known RC2 solver [33] has been available through PySAT, but
       an abstraction capable of calling various engines has remained missing.
           Furthermore, the formalization of the IPAMIR [52] Interface (akin to IPASIR [12] for
       MaxSAT) has provided a common base for stateful MaxSAT, driving applications across
       machine learning, argumentation, and formal verification [30, 38, 40, 67, 65].

 3      The Hermax Library
Taking its name from Hermes, the messenger in Greek mythology who moves between the
realms, Hermax (Hermes + MaxSAT) is an emissary between worlds: the Pythonic world
and the low-level reality of high performance solvers.


3.1     Design Principles and API
Hermax is designed to provide a unified, solver agnostic Python API that adheres to the
IPAMIR interface. IPAMIR enables users to incrementally construct and modify formulas
with irremovable clauses and update the weights of soft literals. Furthermore, it supports
optimization under temporary assumptions, and allows for the optional registration of a
callback. Hermax maps the IPAMIR C interface directly to an abstract Python base class,
IPAMIRSolver. Figure 1 illustrates this equivalence.

   Hermax also introduces abstractions that remain fully compliant with the IPAMIR
contract. For example, while IPAMIR expects unit soft literals, Hermax provides an
add_soft_relaxed helper that handles the introduction of relaxation variables and the
hardening process automatically as well as a get_model for collecting entire solutions.


3.2     Supported Solvers
Hermax categorizes its MaxSAT engines into two families: native incremental solvers that
internally implement the IPAMIR standard, and non-incremental adapters that emulate this
interface through a wrapper layer. At the lowest level, lightweight pybind11 wrappers expose
the C IPAMIR as a Python object. This allows routing formulas in-memory and avoids disk
I/O and parsing bottlenecks. Above these abstractions, Hermax implements high-level solver
classes inheriting from IPAMIRSolver.
    The hermax.incremental module provides direct access to the solvers available through
the MaxSAT incremental competition, primarily: UWrMaxSAT [59], featuring both an
updated Github 1.8 and the 1.4 competition version, as well as EvalMaxSAT [11] and
iMaxHS [51].

                The hermax.non_incremental module groups wrapper adapters used when a backend
            is invoked, emulating an incremental API. These adapters allow solvers like CASHWMax-

            counterparts. Hermax also supports process isolated incomplete MaxSAT solvers that are
            run natively thanks to the hermax.non_incremental.incomplete module, with OpenW-
            BOInc [42], TT-OpenWBO [49], SPB-MaxSAT-c-FPS [68], Loandra [15], and NuWLS-c-
            IBR [41]. For incomplete solvers engineered for one-shot solving, Hermax utilizes processes to
            safely interrupt execution, extract the best known solution, and reclaim memory resources.

 4      A MaxSAT Compiler

Despite the impressive performance of modern MaxSAT solvers, the ecosystem has lacked
a high-level optimization language that targets exportable CNF and integrates with the
plethora of existing solvers. To fix this gap, we introduce a SAT/MaxSAT modelling compiler
with CP primitives. Written in pure Python, it provides the ergonomic abstractions of CP
while guaranteeing immediate resolution to CNF and WCNF. We commit to the order/ladder
encoding [7, 66] for integer variables, which allows the compiler to unlock optimizations
unavailable in other SAT compilation pipelines.
    Most compiler languages operate by constructing an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) repres-
enting the entire problem, which is later flattened and optimized by a staged compilation
pipeline. Our approach discards this paradigm in favor of eager evaluation. The compiler
data flow can be seen in Figure 3.


                                                      Commit
  User                 Model Frontend API            Constraint            Compiler
  Query             Bool, Int, Enum, Vector, etc.                      Encoder Dispatch

                                                                                   CNF Implications

  User                    Solve & Decode               Export        Core Logic & State
 Answer                SAT, MaxSAT, Decoder                       Model, ClauseGroup, Clause


     Figure 3 Data flow pipeline for the eager evaluation compiler architecture.


    Unlike CP-SAT, constraint expressions are quickly resolved into clauses. Furthermore,
our compiler is CNF oriented. We deliberately avoid emitting arbitrary logical circuits (e.g.
those requiring Tseitin or DNF unrolling). This decision ensures that the compiled query
resembles the user-intended model as closely as possible.


4.1     A Constraint Programming Inspired API
The library provides an extensive suite of modelling primitives, including Boolean variables,
order encoded integers, optionally nullable categoricals, and interval variables for scheduling.
These primitives can be organized into vectors and matrices collections that support NumPy
style slicing, flattening, and row/column extraction. At the modelling level, users have access
to various constraints, such as extensional tables, cardinalities (e.g., AMO, ALO, exact-K),
boundary aggregations (max, min), and optimized AllDifferent backends. Additionally, the
API supports algebraic operations, including vector multiplexing, dynamic index resolution
(A = V [B]), floor division (X//c), piecewise functions, among many other functions.

   Typical SAT compilations of affine constraints rely on one-hot encodings (e.g., i i · a=i =
P

encodings to compile these relations directly. Figure 5 illustrates four operations compiled
without auxiliary variables:
1. Scaling (A = 2X): Generates upward implications (x≥k → a≥2k ) and bounds domain
   gaps downward (a≥2k−1 → x≥k ).
2. Shifting (A = S + 2): Mapped as an index shift via exact equivalences (a≥k ↔ s≥k−2 ).
   The double-bordered node a≥2 marks a forced threshold literal (unit clause).
3. Precedence (S ≤ F ): Enforced via monotone implications (s≥k → f≥k ).
4. Maximum (M = max(F, G)): Evaluated across thresholds using binary and ternary
   clauses (m≥k ↔ f≥k ∨ g≥k ).
For reference, compiling A = 2X requires 59 variables and 141 clauses in CPMpy (which uses
one-hot PB encodings); Hermax compiles the same constraint using zero auxiliary variables,
requiring only the 9 original ladder variables and 13 clauses. Consequently, combinatorial
models involving interval variables (e.g. scheduling, routing) avoid expansion overhead.
   This threshold representation extends to constraints such as AllDifferent. Rather than
enforcing O(N 2 ) pairwise inequalities, Hermax materializes exact value literals (x=k ↔
x≥k ∧ ¬x≥k+1 ) and applies At-Most-One constraints across the domains.


4.3        Model Compiler Example
To illustrate the expressivity of the supported language, we model the Capacitated Vehicle
Routing Problem (CVRP). In CVRP, vehicles with uniform capacity must service nodes
with specific demands, starting and ending at a central depot, while minimizing the travel
distance. We will use the Miller-Tucker-Zemlin (MTZ) formulation [47]. We define a Boolean
matrix for edges and a ladder encoded integer vector to track the accumulated load of the
vehicle. The objective function must minimize the travel distance. We also demonstrate how
distance matrices can be dynamically updated to simulate real-time traffic conditions.

                This example illustrates how Hermax bridges modelling and low-level SAT so users build
            constraints using idiomatic Python. In the example, sum() natively lowers to cardinality
            constraints, and matrix slices (e.g., edges.row(i)) integrate with these encoders. Further-
            more, the compiler evaluates arithmetic to minimize the formula size. Unary bounds against
            constants (loads[i] >= demands[i]) are folded at compile time directly into a single literal
            from the ladder encoding, introducing zero overhead.
                For more complex operations, the engine intercepts the expressions to bypass PB encoding.
            The MTZ constraint (Ei,j =⇒ (Li + dj ≤ Lj )) exemplifies this: instead of falling back on
            PB, the dispatcher recognizes the bivariate relation and applies gating at the clause level.
            This lowers the MTZ constraint into a O(|L|) number of ladder implications with binary
            clauses, and with ternary clauses introduced for the conditional.
                The Hermax compiler also abstracts the state of incremental MaxSAT solving. When
            the model changes and the objective function is reassigned, the compiler automatically
            differentiates the new objective expression against the old one. It then issues the delta
            IPAMIR weight modifications required to synchronize the solver’s state. Users can inject

temporary assumptions and query the solver’s assignment using the exact same Python
objects used during formulation. In terms of modelling of the objective functions, multiple
abstractions and strategies are supported:
     Floating point weights: Users specify an integer precision parameter, allowing the
     compiler to automatically scale floating point values into integers.
     Negative weights: The compiler applies the equality −w · x = w · ¬x − w. It translates
     a negative penalty on a literal into a positive penalty on its negation, maintaining the
     negative offset of the reported objective.
     Lexicographic optimization: Hermax provides two optimization strategies. By default,
     it issues multiple consecutive solver calls to iteratively solve and harden each level.
     Alternatively, it performs an automatic transformation that scales and aggregates multi-
     level weights into a single objective level for a one-shot call.


 5      Hermax Availability

Hermax is available under the Apache 2.0 open source license. Hermax officially supports
Windows (with MinGW), Linux, and macOS across both x86 and ARM architectures with
precompiled wheels, which required extensive patching of the integrated solvers.


  Installation: pip install hermax
  Available on PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/hermax/
  Documentation: https://hermax.readthedocs.io/


    While this library lowers the barrier to entry, the reliability of the system remains
dependent on the underlying C++ MaxSAT engines, which may exhibit implementation
bugs [56]. This is important to consider on a tool that will be used by non-SAT experts. Our
test suite uncovered undefined behaviour that only presented itself on some architectures,
which allowed us to patch bugs at the individual solver level that have not manifested
themselves on Linux x86.


 6      Conclusions & Future Work

Hermax connects high-level Python prototyping with high-performance MaxSAT solving
via an IPAMIR interface and an eager CNF/WCNF compiler. Our main contribution is
practical unification: users can model with CP primitives, update objectives and assumptions
incrementally, and target a broad set of MaxSAT engines from the same Python API.
    In terms of solver support, we want to broaden Hermax by integrating modern [35] and
historical solvers [6, 29, 39]. We also want to expand queries to multi-objective optimization
and solution enumeration, potentially using backends like RustSAT.
    As for the compiler, we want to work on evaluating the trade-off between full clause
materialization and the high-level reasoning of native CP solvers, and bring insight into when
each approach is most effective. To support this, we plan to explore alternative encoding
strategies [1] and implement MaxSAT-specific preprocessing techniques [14] before solving.
    We also want to explore portfolio strategies across different supported solvers. Specifically,
making use of new 2026 MaxSAT Evaluation lower-bound reporting while solving to merge
the capabilities of complete and incomplete solvers in a single call.
